audio_caption: The audio clip begins with an orchestral piece featuring a dramatic, suspenseful tone. This fades out to be replaced by a male speaker, who introduces himself as Professor Jim Kaffi and announces that the topic is chapter six on "astronomical instruments". Then, the audio switches to instrumental music again, similar in style and tone to the intro piece.

The audio clip features a male speaker introducing the Hubble Space Telescope and its history since 1990, mentioning its eventual replacement. The speaker points out recognizable features of the Orion Nebula, such as Orion's Belt, shoulders, and feet, explaining the nebula's position within the belt. He also notes the nebula's varied appearance at different wavelengths.

The audio clip begins with speech about pre-telescopic observatories, specifically mentioning Machu Picchu and Stonehenge, spoken by a male speaker with an instructional tone. He goes on to explain the formation of an image by a simple lens. An animal breathing sound is heard.

The audio clip starts with a male speaker explaining the difference between refracting and reflecting telescopes. He explains that refracting telescopes bend light through a lens, while reflecting telescopes reflect light off a mirror through another mirror, then through an eyepiece. The speaker then mentions different areas of focus with reflecting telescopes.

The clip begins with a male speaker discussing "the aperture" and "eyepiece", along with focusing "within the mirror itself". He then moves on to mention "a very large telescope mirror" to be used by the "European Southern Observatory's very large telescope". The speaker has a clear and informative tone. There is a brief pause.

The audio clip appears to feature a single male speaker discussing astronomical instruments and telescopes, expressing that they have "interesting names." He mentions the "Palomar 5-meter reflector" and the "Gemini North 8-meter telescope." His tone seems informative and slightly enthusiastic. The speaker then states a thought, implying that "36 eyes are better than one."

The audio clip begins with a single male speaker discussing telescope construction, mentioning the use of "segmented mirrors" that are "glued together to make one large mirror," specifically for the "Keck telescope in Hawaii" in a conversational and informative tone.

The clip begins with a single male speaker discussing "George Hale" and his work with telescopes. He mentions that the "largest refractor bending telescope in the world" is a 40-inch telescope located in Chicago. He then states that most observatories are located "as far high up on a mountain as they can go."

The audio presents a single male speaker describing a "high and dry site" in Chile's Atacama Desert for the European Southern Observatory. He goes on to explain how "pistons" are used to correct telescope mirrors for the atmosphere. He then mentions CCDs in cameras and how they are "sensitive to light." Following this, he notes the ability to see hands in a bag in the infrared, which gives off heat radiation. Finally, he describes a prism spectrometer, which "will split up the light from white light into its colorful rainbow." The speaker maintains an informative and descriptive tone throughout.

The audio clip begins with speech, a male speaker saying "Here's the first radio telescope", describing a basic telescope and mentioning its use by Jansky in discovering radio radiation from the Milky Way. He then transitions to describing what a radio image looks like, pointing out a galaxy in the middle and two lobes far out in space, with jets coming from the image. The audio ends with a distinct click sound.

The audio begins with a male speaker discussing the Green Bank Telescope in West Virginia, noting its large size. He then mentions the Large Millimeter Array in Chile and the possibility of using radio telescopes across the Earth, linking them to function as a giant radio dish. He then refers to the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico, describing it as the world's largest radio and radar dish.

The clip begins with a male speaker discussing placing observatories into the upper atmosphere. He references "Sophia," explaining it helps bypass most of the earth's water vapor, which blocks infrared light. The clip concludes with a brief musical interlude, possibly jazz, with a calming tone.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker describing how the Spitzer Space Telescope captures infrared images and then moves on to Hubble's Ultra-Deep Field, explaining that this area allows us to see back 13 billion years. He continues discussing the Chandra X-ray satellite and its function. Finally, he mentions the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope launch in 2021, all in a factual and informative tone.

The audio features a male speaker discussing rigorous testing and mentioning the European Extremely Large Telescope under construction in Chile. Following this, there is a brief encouragement to enjoy an episode, transitioning into a mention of ten-minute astronomy. The speaker then suggests exploring videos and subscribing to the channel. Subsequently, music with an unspecified genre or style begins to play.
